source.title: Attribution-Guided Distillation of Matryoshka Sparse Autoencoders
source.authors: Cristina P. Martin-Linares; Jonathan P. Ling

record.tranche_reason: The study examines how consistently SAE features are selected and reused across training cycles and sparsity settings. It also qualifies feature stability: it freezes encoder directions, but reinitializes biases and decoder weights, so identical latent behavior is not guaranteed.
record.gate_note: The study does not test toy-model superposition or measure overlapping, nearly orthogonal feature geometry. Its own results on repeated core selection, core usefulness, and SAEBench feature metrics bear on SAE-feature recovery and stability. Statements about prior SAE pathologies attributed to other work are not recorded as results.
record.test_reason: This is a methods paper. It proposes DMSAE, a way to train SAEs by distilling a frozen core of encoder directions, and reports that method's performance against Matryoshka and BatchTopK baselines on SAEBench. The cross-cycle 'carryover' is a property of its own pipeline: selected encoder directions are copied and frozen into the next cycle, so re-selection is partly built in. It is not an independent test of whether SAE features are stable or canonical across training runs. No toy-model, polysemanticity, neuron-spread or 1-D-versus-multi-D result is reported. SAEs are used as the tool, and the results concern the method's own value.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude that attribution-guided distillation yields a 197-latent core on Gemma-2-2B layer 12 and improves multiple SAEBench metrics over Matryoshka baselines. They present this as a practical route toward feature consistency across runs and sparsity levels. They note that consistency holds only at the level of encoder directions, not identical latent behaviour. The paraphrase should add that AutoInterp drops at the lowest sparsities.
record.recipe_differences: The paper develops attribution-guided distillation of Matryoshka sparse autoencoders; it does not reproduce the toy-model superposition method. It transfers and freezes selected SAE encoder directions across training cycles.
record.method_sensitivity: Core carryover depends strongly on target sparsity: k=20-80 gives little carryover, k=160 and k=320 substantial carryover, and k=640 degenerates. AutoInterp also drops sharply at the lowest tested sparsities. The core selection uses gradient × activation attribution with τ=0.9.

fits_no_version.finding: In the DMSAE pipeline, re-selection of frozen core latents across cycles depends strongly on sparsity. There is little carryover at k=20-80, substantial carryover at k=160/320, and collapse at k=640.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Attribution-selected SAE core directions re-persist across retraining only in an intermediate sparsity regime.

fits_no_version.finding: A distilled core stays active during retraining, while a random core of the same size is driven toward zero activity.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Attribution-distilled SAE encoder directions remain useful for reconstruction under retraining, unlike random directions.

fits_no_version.finding: DMSAE improves absorption and RAVEL over Matryoshka SAEs, but AutoInterp drops at the lowest sparsities.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Freezing a distilled core of encoder directions improves some SAEBench metrics at an interpretability cost at low sparsity.

record.problems: The experiments use only Gemma-2-2B layer 12 activations. Most benchmark outcomes are described qualitatively in text or shown in figures without numerical values or uncertainty estimates. The authors note that gradient × activation attribution may be suboptimal, that multi-cycle distillation is computationally expensive, and that freezing encoder directions does not guarantee identical latent behavior across retrainings.
record.rows_left_out: No additional claim-relevant results were omitted. Other SAEBench metrics and attribution-threshold results were not recorded because the text does not connect them to the listed claim versions.

untested.parts: All of it: no toy models, no geometry, no sparsity-dependent transition.
All of it: no neuron-level polysemanticity or capacity competition.
Does not measure whether features are spread across neurons. SAE recovery is assumed, and the paper only compares SAE variants.
No independent test of completeness, stability across unconstrained seeds, or canonicality. Consistency is imposed by freezing encoder directions.

record.verdict_notes: The reader labelled this paper as T5 testing V4 and V5. That is overreach. The carryover and core results are artefacts of a pipeline that freezes transferred directions, and the SAEBench rows compare the study's own method with baselines. Background claims about SAE instability are cited from Paulo & Belrose and Leask et al., not shown here. All figure results are qualitative in the text, with no uncertainty reported.

versions.untested_parts: No toy-network test, superposition geometry, sparsity-dependent geometric transition, or regular geometric arrangement.
No test of neuron polysemanticity or whether feature competition for capacity causes it.
No test of alternative causes of polysemantic neurons or whether polysemanticity indicates superposition.
Tests SAE feature metrics on Gemma-2-2B layer 12 activations, not whether model features are spread across neurons or whether recovered features are complete.
Tests repeated selection and transfer of encoder directions, not whether SAE features are complete or canonical units of the model's representation.
Uses encoder weight vectors as directions, but does not compare one-dimensional with multidimensional feature representations.
